ARC 100.title: Introduction to Ancient Near Eastern Archaeology
ARC 100.description: An overview of the ancient Near East, this course examines its history, geography, art, and architecture. Beginning with the development of agriculture in the Neolithic period, it traces the rise of urban societies in Iraq and the great empires of Mesopotamia, Assyria, Babylonia, and Sumer. Thematic topics include culture, politics, writing, religion, and gender roles. Attention is also given to neighboring civilizations such as the Achaemenid Empire, Anatolia, the Hittites, Egypt, and the Phoenicians.

It maps heritage studies within history, archaeology, tourism, sociology, anthropology, economics, development, philosophy, international relations, and law. BUS 112.title: Introduction to Business
BUS 112.description: This course is designed to help students understand the many ways in which business affects people and society. Students will learn the essential components of the business world and the organizations that exist in it. Students will discover why location is such a significant force in society and prepare themselves for careers in the business sector. Prerequisite: ASP level five.

BUS 212.title: Professional Development and Career Planning
BUS 212.description: This course is designed to improve your understanding of professional development (PD) and career planning (CD). By combining theory, research, and practice, we will examine key topics related to PD & CD, such as the framework for understanding PD & CD, developing and practicing career-enhancing skills, and functions of career planning (e.g., mentoring and coaching personnel and conducting career assessments). Prerequisite: BUS 112.

BUS 215.title: Business Law
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
BUS 215.description: This course is an introductory course dealing with legal principles and procedures. It is an introduction to contract law. The main objective of this course is to introduce students to business transactions and to develop an understanding of the legal framework of business- the basic principles of the law which form the legal framework for business activity including applicable statutes, contracts, and agency. The course will equip students with the necessary knowledge to choose the form of business entity, structure ownership, raise money, handle operational liabilities, protect intellectual property, go global, and go public. Special attention will be given to Iraqi Company Law No. 21 as amended in 2004 which aims at protecting creditors from fraud, protect shareholders from conflicts of interest.

BUS 250.title: Business Statistics
BUS 250.description: Business Statistics is a critical tool for decision-making in business and economic situations. Students will learn the basics of data description, ideas associated with probability distributions, and inferential techniques, including confidence intervals and hypothesis testing for parameter values. Concepts of linear regression will be introduced through line fitting to bivariate data. Prerequisite: BUS 112.

BUS 305.title: Effective Communication in Bus

BUS 375.title: Internship

Internships offer the opportunity to “try out” a career while gaining relevant experience and professional connections. Internships are completed under the guidance of an on-site supervisor and a faculty sponsor, who, in combination with the student, will create a framework for learning and reflection. Prerequisite: Complete a minimum of 81 credits.

ENT 310.title: Foundations of Entrepreneurship I: Business Discovery and Assessment
ENT 310.description: This course introduces students to the foundational process of discovering and evaluating viable new business opportunities. Rather than relying on entrepreneurial intuition, the course emphasizes a structured, iterative approach used by successful entrepreneurs to identify market openings, assess organizational capabilities, and determine whether a venture can create and capture value. Students learn how to evaluate industry conditions, analyze value creation, and assess the financial feasibility of proposed ventures. Through case studies and student-driven projects, participants apply these concepts to real business ideas. The course culminates in a comprehensive business feasibility study. It is designed for both aspiring business students interested in entrepreneurship and non-business students seeking innovative ways to create sustainable opportunities in their chosen fields. Prerequisite: MGT 201.

ENT 320.title: Foundations of Entrepreneurshi
ENT 320.description: The main focus of this course is to consider and discuss entrepreneurial processes in established firms as well as newly created ventures. It focuses less on the 'how' of entrepreneurship, but on the 'what' and the 'why'. It considers theories on the nature of entrepreneurship that explain entrepreneurial success and how entrepreneurship relates to innovation. Over the course of the semester, students will work in teams to work on case studies, culminating in an end-of-term individual case development and presentation. Students work individually or in groups to launch an opportunity business as a minimum viable product (MVP) related to Baghdad-area industries. Success is measured in launching an MVP, gathering customer feedback, and pitching to guest investors. Prerequisite: ENT 310.

HUM 101.title: Introduction to Humanities
HUM 101.description: This course explores the essential question: What does it mean to be human? Students will examine how human identity and experience are expressed across ten disciplines of the humanities, including literature, philosophy, art, music, theater, cinema, religion, archaeology, history, and media. The course highlights Middle Eastern heritage, with special focus on Iraqi UNESCO World Heritage sites, and integrates global perspectives.

LAW 101.title: Introduction to the Study of Law (Law Theory; Right Theory):
LAW 101.description: This course is introductory. The course aims to provide a basic but fundamental understanding of the nature of law, legal rules, legal persons, and legal rights. The course topics include the concept, characteristics, and functions of legal rules, the division or branches of law, sources of law, and the interpretation and application of legal rules. This course also deals with legal personality and classification of legal rights (civil rights, property rights, human rights, etc.). Language of Instruction: English.

LAW 102.title: Legal Terminology
LAW 102.description: The course covers legal English's key vocabulary and emphasizes legal terms used in legal courses in the College of Law. The course emphasizes the mastery of legal vocabulary to enhance students' proficiency in legal communication across multiple areas of law. The course also provides basic instruction in legal principles, including contracts, torts, legal procedure, constitutional law, and administrative law. Course materials include legal dictionaries focusing on the terms that students are expected to master. This course is a prerequisite for all second year and higher-level law courses. Language of Instruction: English.

LAW 103.title: Legal Reasoning and Writing
LAW 103.description: This course teaches students to make professional legal writing decisions and to think and argue simultaneously like a lawyer or legal adviser. The act of writing requires a law professional to test, analyze, structure, and express thoughts and ideas with clarity and precision. This course examines basic concepts of law and legal reasoning. The course focuses on the writing process and how to use language as a professional tool. Students are introduced to several types of written legal documents, including predictive writing and persuasive writing. Students also learn to “brief” cases and prepare memoranda of law, appellate briefs, and client communication. Language of Instruction: English. Prerequisites / Corequisites: LAW 101 and LAW 102.

LAW 104.title: Criminology and Penology
LAW 104.description: This course provides students with an introduction and overview of the system of criminal justice in operation. The course begins with a survey of the sources, philosophy, and role of law in society, and provides a brief introduction to different legal traditions and systems. The course also examines those factors that distinguish civil, criminal, and social justice. Students learn the definitions of a "crime", “evidence,” and social responses to crimes. A broad survey of the policing and prosecution, Adjudication, sentencing, and corrections provide students with a basic understanding of the administration of criminal justice. Language of Instruction: English. Adjudication, sentencing, and corrections provide students with a basic understanding of the administration of criminal justice. Language of Instruction: English. Course Prerequisites: None.

LAW 105.title: Introduction to Islamic Law (Sharia)
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 105.description: This course familiarizes students with the sources, nature, and functions of Islamic law in a historical context. It provides a framework for thinking about social realities and institutional structures that help shape Islamic law and explains the legal adaptations within Islamic law over time. The power, history, and theory of the Islamic Legal System are examined with particular emphasis on the development of the various schools of thought within Islamic law, and the interaction between the Sharia and recently promulgated Civil Codes. This course also encourages comparative legal analysis to assess generalizations about law typically formulated by Western legal traditions. Language of Instruction: Arabic.

LAW 106.title: Constitutional Law
LAW 106.description: This course is divided into three parts. The first part examines the general constitutional theories of diverse states and political systems (Theories of States). Part two examines the nature of constitutions, a survey of the US, French, and EU constitutions, as well as the relationships among the executive, legislative, and judicial areas of government. Constitutional principles, rights, and civil liberties are also discussed, considering the long tradition of diverse philosophical and theoretical perceptions (Theories of Constitutions or Constitutionalism). Part three of the course examines the history, formation, basic principles, and structure of the Iraqi constitution, including its current application. The theories and practices of judicial review and federal and unitary states are also discussed. Language of Instruction: English & Arabic. Prerequisites / Corequisites: LAW 101 and LAW 102.

LAW 112.title: History of Roman Law and Hammurabi Law
LAW 112.description: Contemporary laws emerge from the long-term development of diverse legal systems, and a variety of sources and conceptions of law. Historically, the Romano-Germanic legal system is the group of legal ideas and systems ultimately derived from the core principles of the Code of Justinian. This course examines Rome’s political and legal system, the legal status of the individual in Roman Law, and the rules that regulate financial relations in Roman Law. The course also examines Hammurabi's Law, which reflected legal articles from multiple legal systems (public Law and Private Law). In particular, the sources and key features of Hammurabi Law, as well as the relevant governance and administrative systems, financial and commercial legislation, and the penal system. Language of Instruction: English. Prerequisites / Corequisites: LAW101 and LAW102.

LAW 220.title: Civil Law (Obligations Theory)
LAW 220.description: This course aims to provide students with an understanding of the foundational principles of ‘obligations’ in the Civil Law and Common Law System from a comparative perspective. The course examines the concepts employed in creating and enforcing different types of obligations. Students will be able to differentiate between the sources and foundations of obligations in contract and delict/tort in Private Law, and identify the essential elements of the formation of contracts and certain other requirements (form and content), which must be satisfied to make contracts legally enforceable. Vitiating factors, such as avoidance, discharge, termination, and remedies for breach, are also discussed. The course investigates unilateral contract/legal transactions and non-contractual liability, specifically the delictual/tortuous liability resulting from the wrongful/harmful acts of others. The course discusses theoretical foundations, analyzes legal issues, and presents hypothetical scenarios to promote student participation and active engagement in the learning process. Language of Instruction: English & Arabic. Prerequisites / Corequisites: LAW 101.

LAW 221.title: Administrative Law
LAW 221.description: This course provides students with an understanding of the foundational concepts and principles of administrative law and public administration. The development and evolution of administration in civil as well as common law countries is explained. The course also provides an understanding of how administrative law functions and allows students to dissect the characteristics of administrative law, the forms and functions of administrative organizations, and the classification and objectives of administrative actions. Key concepts and issues, such as administrative contracts and public utilities, the legal personality of administrative organs, and types and limitations of administrative control, are covered. The course investigates the methods of administrative decision-making as well as their implementation and enforcement in practice. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisite / Corequisite: LAW106.

LAW 221L.title: Analytical Chemistry Lab
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 221L.description: A laboratory course to accompany Analytical Chemistry. Prerequisite or Corequisite: CHE 221.

LAW 224.title: Civil Law (Provisions of Obligations)
LAW 224.description: This course builds on the understanding of civil law obligations provided in the course LAW 220, specifically by focusing on legal provisions in the Iraqi Civil Code of 1951. The course provides a brief reflection on the formation of a contract and its essential elements. It then discusses in detail the effects and dissolution of the contract. The course provides a brief reflection on legal provisions relating to unilateral and illegal/prohibited contracts and covers delictual/tortuous liability for ‘unlawful acts and gains without justification (restitution/unjust enrichment). Further, the course deals with conditions and terms in a contract, where each is defined in terms of types, effects, and expiration. The plurality of parties in contract and transfer of obligation, whether by assignment of rights or assignment of debt, are discussed. Finally, the course discusses in detail the discharge of obligation either by way of performance, renewal, delegation, or by impossibility of performance and the statute of limitations. Language of Instruction: English & Arabic. Prerequisite: LAW 220.

LAW 227.title: Personal Status Law (Marriage & Divorce)
LAW 227.description: This course examines topics such as marriage contracts and their purpose, provisions of engagement, terms of the contract and full capacity, lack of capacity, incomplete capacity, forced marriage, registration of the marriage contract, and proof of marriage. Definitions of guardianship in the marriage contract and the reasons for the prohibition in the Marriage contracts are covered. In addition, the course covers matters relating to dowry and women's entitlement to the entire dowry. It also deals with definitions and conditions for divorce and alimony, elements of alimony, and Personal Status Law for Non-Muslims. Language of Instruction: Arabic. Prerequisite: LAW 105. .

LAW 230.title: Criminal Law: General Theory
LAW 230.description: This course deals with defining the concept of crime, explaining classifications of crimes, and distinguishing between criminal offenses, disciplinary offenses, and civil wrongs. The concepts and importance of the rule of law and the principle of legality as they relate to crimes and penalties are discussed. This includes clarification of the principles that govern the application of the Penal Code in terms of place and time and the validity of those rules. Also discussed are the nature and elements of crime -the physical element and the moral element-, including an explanation of attempts to commit a crime and criminal participation in the offense. An examination of the impediments to criminal responsibility and the reasons for legally established permissibility will also be explored. Language of Instruction: English & Arabic. Prerequisite: LAW 104.

LAW 240.title: Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law
LAW 240.description: This course covers various aspects of human rights law, including theories, sources, traditions, and legal guarantees, including the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Covenants, and third-generation rights. The course deals with regional systems of human rights and contemporary issues around human rights, such as the impact of globalization and new technologies, terrorism, and human rights in Iraq. The first part of the course provides an overview of the prosecution of human rights violations at the international level, specifically at the international criminal courts and tribunals. The course examines the fundamentals of international humanitarian law, specifically the laws of war, rules concerning cyberattacks, and the intersections with human rights law. The course also comprehends the Geneva Conventions, the Rome Statute, and the International Criminal Court, with a focus on mechanisms for the implementation of International Humanitarian Law and the principles of international criminal law. Language of Instruction: English. Prerequisite: LAW 101.

LAW 260.title: Financial Legislation and Tax Law
LAW 260.description: This course provides an overview of Iraqi fiscal policy, domestic tax codes, and related legislation. Because fiscal policy is used to influence the economy, the course covers government borrowing, public debt, and the government’s role in expanding or contracting GDP. The international part of the course focuses on principles of international taxation where enterprises are subject to taxation in more than one Nation State. The Model Tax Convention of the OECD is used to explain jurisdiction to tax, permanent establishment, transfer pricing, and asset classifications. MTC is also used to explain Double Tax Treaties and methods of tax relief, such as exemption and credit. OECD reforms such as BEPS 1.0 and 2.0 are covered, time permitting. The emphasis is upon understanding international tax strategies employed by company groups and the efforts of Nation States to generate tax revenue consistent with the principles of international trade, economic growth, and avoidance of double taxation. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Course Prerequisites: LAW 106.

LAW 280.title: Commercial and Corporate Law
LAW 280.description: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of key principles in commercial law, including commercial, transport, and insurance contracts. The course uses the United Nations Convention on the International Sale of Goods as an instance of international law, since Iraq is a signatory to the CISG. Incoterms and documentary credits are defined. The course also covers corporate law, encompassing definitions, types, characteristics, procedural rules, and legal documents governing company formation and registration. Additionally, the course addresses legal issues concerning foreign company branches. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Course Prerequisites: LAW 220.Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: Law 220

Vis Moot, the Saudi Arbitration Competition, mediation, and negotiation events, are used to simulate dispute resolution. Students gain experience in pretrial, trial, and post-conviction matters under the close supervision of faculty. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Co/Prerequisites: LAW 280.

LAW 300.title: Legal Internship
LAW 300.description: Legal internships are off-campus experiential learning activities designed to enhance students' skills through practical practice in legal areas. Internships close the gap between theory and practice in the legal profession. This course enables students to shape future legal aspirations to meet individual needs. LAW 300 offers students an opportunity to gain knowledge and skills through work experience in legal firms, and other legal entities (National, Regional, and International). Specific Learning Outcomes are determined and assessed by the Faculty Internship Advisor and Work-site Supervisor. Internship practices are directly aligned with the student’s legal studies program and offer exceptional legal experiences. Course Prerequisites: Completion of LAW 220, LAW 224, LAW 240, and a total of 50 credits

A holistic study of the meaning of inheritance, its causes, and provisions is undertaken. In addition, an explanation of the terms and conditions of forming valid wills, as well as the distribution of estate assets among heirs, is explored, as well as the Personal Status Law for Non-Muslims. Language of Instruction: Arabic. Course Prerequisites: LAW 227 Prerequisites: LAW 227 Language of Instruction: Arabic.

LAW 330.title: Civil Law Special Contracts
LAW 330.description: This course introduces students to the key concepts and theories of special contracts, which include sales, exchange, electronic, and donative contracts as well as leases and rental agreements, loans, deposits, insurance and maintenance contracts, and subcontracts. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Course Prerequisites: LAW 224.

LAW 331.title: Civil Procedure: Evidence, Execution, and Bar Association Law
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 331.description: This course introduces the rules and principles that govern procedure in civil litigation, personal jurisdiction matters, and subject-matter jurisdiction. This course also deals with such topics as pleading; joinder of claims and parties; summary judgment, and the law of prior adjudication, including claim and issue preclusion, class actions, discovery, summary judgment, directed verdict, res judicata, collateral estoppel, and the appeal process. The Laws of Evidence are likewise covered, including means of establishing rights, doctrines, and methods of proof, the role of the judge in proof in Islamic jurisprudence and comparative systems, and the modern role of the judge and litigants. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Co/Prerequisites: LAW 330.

LAW 334.title: AJ — Administrative Judiciary
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 334.description: AJ — Administrative Judiciary: This course deals with the principle of legality and the scope of the discretionary power of the administration, the theory of sovereign acts, political, administrative, and judicial oversight, and the administrative judiciary in Iraq. There is discussion of the unified and dual judiciary and administrative disputes that fall within the jurisdiction of different judiciaries, as well as examination of administrative lawsuits, and the concept of a lawsuit quashing an administrative decision according to Iraqi law. The course also covers implementation of administrative decisions and evidence in administrative cases. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: LAW 221 DL

LAW 354.title: Penal Code: Specific Crimes and Cybersecurity
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 354.description: LAW 354— Penal Code: Specific Crimes and Cybersecurity: This course delves into a curated selection of criminal offenses, including Crimes against public trust like counterfeiting currency and forgery of documents, Crimes violating official duties such as bribery, crimes of abuse of authority, and crimes against public morals. Moreover, it addresses Crimes endangering human life and freedom, encompassing assault, murder, crimes against physical integrity, abortion crimes, crimes against honor and dignity, offenses against property like theft, as well as Crimes of betrayal of trust and fraud. Additionally, students will acquire skills to formulate comprehensive cybersecurity policies and fortify cybersecurity frameworks to mitigate risks. Ethics and Policy in Cyberspace constitute vital components of this course. Practical sessions involving the analysis of Court of Appeal case law are also incorporated into the course. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: Law 106 & Law 230

LAW 390.title: Public International Law
LAW 390.description: The course familiarizes students with the foundational aspects of public international law, encompassing the origins, and sources, such as treaties, customary norms, General Principles of Law, and Subsidiaries of International Law. Additionally, it delves into the topics concerning international law subjects and states (including their emergence, kinds, and recognition). Furthermore, the course covers themes like the International Responsibility of States, Diplomatic Protection, and International Succession. Moreover, it addresses peaceful means for resolving international disputes, encompassing the Judicial Settlement of International Disputes, focusing on the International Court of Justice, its composition, and Jurisdiction. Practical sessions related to ICJ case law are also integrated into the course. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: Law 240.

Jessup Competition and other competitions in the field of international law by teaching previous competition cases. It enables them to understand the fundamentals of international law and the mechanism for solving international problems, as well as develop their skills in writing legal memoranda and pleading for claimants and respondents. the purpose of this course is to prepare students for participation in Philip C. Jessup Competition and others. They gain experience in pretrial, trial, and post-conviction matters under the close supervision of faculty.

LAW 400.title: Labor Law and Social Security
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 400.description: This course entails a study of general principles in labor legislation in terms of its definition, importance, development, international organization, sources, independence, scope of application of such laws, as well as individual work contracts (elements, duration, termination) and the regulation of collective labor relations and the settlement of labor disputes. This course also deals with Social Security Law, the financial system for social security in Iraq, health insurance, disability, partial disability, and compensation. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: LAW 224.

LAW 422.title: Islamic Jurisprudence
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 422.description: This course deals with the definition of Sharia and jurisprudence, the need for legislation, characteristics, and principles of Islamic jurisprudence and Sharia, the relationship of Sharia with other laws and the law, the history and development of Islamic jurisprudence to the present era, doctrines of jurisprudence and the theory of eligibility and its provisions. This course deals with the definition of the legal ruling: its definition and its divisions, the fundamental rules: general and specific, absolute and restricted, and the theory of interpretation of texts in science Usul al-Fiqh, Ijtihad: Conditions, Place and Ruling. Tradition: its rules and controls, inconsistency. Objectives of Islamic Sharia. Language of Instruction: Arabic. Course Prerequisites: LAW 320.

LAW 431.title: Civil Law: Real Rights and Ancillary
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 431.description: This course deals with the laws governing all aspects of real property and the creation of rights. Additional topics include ownership rights, real property contracts, real property mortgages, the statute of fraud problems, conveyancing, and adverse possession also discussed as In-kind insurance. Also covered are all aspects of official mortgage contracts, possessory pledges, and franchise rights. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: LAW330.

LAW 440.title: Private International Law and
LAW 440.description: This course starts from the general historical development of the doctrines of Private International Law, then covers its relationship with general International Law, general principles of nationality in comparative law, and the state’s freedom to regulate nationality and citizenship. The course also deals with the status of foreigners in terms of the general principles of organizing the legal status of foreigners. The course examines the conflict of laws theory: rules of conflict, classification, and qualification, public policy, and rules of foreign law. recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments, Rules governing international arbitral proceedings, and arbitral jurisdiction. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Course Co/Prerequisites: LAW 431, & LAW 390.

LAW 456.title: Criminal Investigation and Forensic
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LAW 456.description: This course deals with the importance and development of practical criminal investigation, criminal investigatory bodies, their tasks and functions, the characteristics of the criminal investigator, the procedural and substantive rules in the field of investigation and detection of crimes, and the use of legal and technical methods to obtain evidence. The course also aims to introduce how to use various legitimate scientific and technical means in the field of research, investigation of truth, and analysis of effects on crime scenes, whether solid, synthetic, or human gaseous liquid and matching lines. To detect forgery and analyze physical and microscopic traces, hair, fibers, threads, soil, and rocks. It also deals with the definition of auxiliary sciences for forensic sciences such as forensic medicine and its technical foundations, forensic chemistry, especially DNA fingerprinting and fingerprints, and how to deal with various cases such as miscarriage, sudden death, injuries, and their types, and burns. And their types, sexual crimes, personality investigation, drowning suffocation, wounds, burns, and their degree, and the causes of various injuries that lead to death or disability, forgery, counterfeiting, poison, and drugs. Language of Instruction: English. Course Prerequisites: LAW 354, Co/requisites LAW 455.

LAW 460.title: Practicum
LAW 460.description: This course integrates academic theory with practical applications, emphasizing case studies and hands-on projects in diverse legal fields. Designed for AUIB students, visiting students, and legal practitioners alike, it offers a flexible selection of courses to accommodate individual schedules and interests. Some suggested courses are Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), Women and International Human Rights, and Principles of Legislative Drafting in Law. Language of instruction: Arabic and English. Course Prerequisites: Completion of 60 credits.

LAW 461.title: Commercial Papers and Banking
LAW 461.description: This course introduces the student to the most important principles of commercial law, commercial contracts, banking operations, and the provisions of private companies and public companies. It also covers the procedural rules related to the preparation of corporate contracts and how to register them. The course will also deal with the definition of commercial papers and their types, the bill of exchange, promissory note and check, and knowledge of the provisions of each of them in terms of creating the paper, the commitment of the signatories to it, its circulation, its acceptance, the payment of its value, how the holder returns to the obligors of the commercial paper and the fall of the lawsuits resulting from it by prescription. The course also explores key aspects of banking law, including banking operations and services, the role of banks in issuing, accepting, and processing commercial papers, banking regulations, and compliance, and the relationship between banks and their customers in commercial transactions. Language of Instruction: English and Arabic. Prerequisites: LAW 280.

LAW 499.title: Capstone
LAW 499.description: The Capstone Seminar is a seminar in which students utilize the knowledge and skills gained through their law degree program studies to create a culminating work that critically addresses a problem in a field of law of their choosing. The students produce a Capstone of 3000-5000 words that presents a position on a relevant legal problem, supports the position with legal literature, analyzes and tests the proposed solution, and discusses the finding. Each student will be assigned a faculty member to provide the student with guidance and feedback during the process. Language of Instruction: English. Course Prerequisites: Completion 103 credits.

LDR 640.title: Leadership
LDR 640.description: This course provides a comprehensive overview of leadership theories, styles, and practices. Students will critically evaluate leadership approaches in diverse organizational contexts and develop their own leadership philosophy. The course emphasizes ethical leadership, influence, motivation, and building high-performing teams. Prerequisites: MGT 600 (Recommended) Key Topics: • Leadership theories and models • Leadership styles and behaviors • Motivation and influence • Ethical and responsible leadership • Leading teams and organizations • Leadership development and self-awareness

LIT 101.title: Introduction to World Literature
LIT 101.description: This course examines various literary genres and forms (short stories, mainly). Schools of literary criticism are introduced, thereby enabling learners to appreciate and analyze the literature they read. Works by prominent authors are closely examined: Gabriel Garcia Marquez, Kate Chopin, Graham Greene, Ernest Hemingway, Nadine Gordimer, Chinua Achebe, VS Naipaul, Lutfia al-Dulaimi, Edwidge Danticat, Henrik Ibsen, Naguib Mahfouz, Mario Vargas Llosa, Yukio Mishima, Anna Akhmatova, Sophocles, and others.

LIT 201.title: Introduction to Literary Analysis
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 201.description: Learners learn how to react to and analyze poetry, drama and fiction in this course. This is by means of interpretation in the broad sense. This is through employing secondary criticism and according to theoretical frameworks. As a result, students will develop intellectual practices required to employ effective critical thinking skills. They will also attentively, write and speak cogently, and distinguish and interrogate cultural behaviors and attitudes evident in the literature studied in the course. Prerequisite: ENL 101

LIT 220.title: British Literature Survey I
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 220.description: This a survey of major works in British literature from the Old English period to the late eighteenth century, with emphasis on literary forms, genres, and themes. To prevent anachronistic interpretation, the writings are interpreted in the appropriate linguistic, cultural, and historical contexts. Authors include Shakespeare, William Blake, John Donne, John Milton, Locke and others. Prerequisite: ENL 101

LIT 221.title: American Literature Survey I
LIT 221.description: This course is specifically aimed at providing and inculcating the learner with background and context relating to the social underpinnings of US society. It starts by treating the “captivity” narrative of Mary Rowlandson, then Jonathan Edwards’s “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God.” It then treats the essays of Ralph Waldo Emerson, then Harriet Jacobs’ slave narrative. The learners are also introduced to the short stories of Nathaniel Hawthorne and the poetry of Emily Dickinson. Prerequisite: ENL 101.

LIT 240.title: British Literature Survey II
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 240.description: This is an overview study of major works of British literature from the Romantic Era to the present, focusing on thematic concerns and aesthetic innovations within British literary production in relation to the socio-historic development of the cultures of Great Britain and its Commonwealth. The works of Charles Dickens, including A Tale of Two Cities, are featured in this course, as are the writings of Rudyard Kipling, including Kim. Prerequisite: LIT 101.

LIT 241.title: American Literature Survey II
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 241.description: This class will examine the social, historical, political and cultural ideas seen, sustained and critiqued in representative American texts. Course materials will include traditional and popular readings, all of which typify American society and culture. Genres ranging from short stories, novellas, and essays, to plays and poetry will be studied, with particular attention to themes such as the “American Dream,” Nature and the Environment, Gender, Race, and Ethnicity, and Religion and Society. Prerequisite: LIT 101.

LIT 242.title: World Literature Survey III
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 242.description: This course examines the works of some of the most famous and influential American authors such as Mark Twain (The Adventures of Tom Sawyer and The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn), Alexis deTocqueville (Democracy in America), Edgar Allan Poe (The Pit and the Pendulum, The Fall of the House of Usher, and The Mask of the Red Death, and The Raven) and O.Henry (The Gift of the Magi). Prerequisite: LIT 101.

LIT 315.title: Survey of Arabic Literature
LIT 315.description: To examine life in Baghdad Belles Lettres, the Book of Misers, by Al-Jaahidh (Al-Jahiz) provides an insightful look into Baghdad society during the Golden Age of Arabic literature. Social class, tribal structure, ethics and more specific to the society of the day here in Baghdad will be examined and discussed objectively. To learn about global historiography, the learners in this course will absorb and analyze English translations of the Muqaddimah [Prolegomena], ("Introduction"), by Ibn Khaldun. Prerequisite: LIT 201.

LIT 320.title: Shakespeare
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 320.description: Since Shakespeare wrote plays about the wider human experience, this course has a significant cross-cultural relevance and “Purpose of Mission.” For it, the prime and recurrent focus will be on themes (such as ambition, the nature of evil, and considerations of race and gender) explored in the tragedies of Macbeth, Hamlet, and Othello. Shakespeare’s reading and interpretation of history (through plays like Henry V) will also be examined, as will some of his famous sonnets. Prerequisite: LIT 201.

Prerequisite: LIT 201.

By featuring outstanding fantasy works, the themes implied in recent fiction are placed into more objective context. Among those selected will be the works of C.S. Lewis, (The Lion, The Witch and The Wardrobe), both The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings, by J.R.R. Tolkien and Fahrenheit 451 by Ray Bradbury, and other important writings. Prerequisite: LIT 201.

LIT 337.title: 20th Century and Contemporary Middle Eastern Literature (in translation)
LIT 337.description: This is a seminar course about recent local literary output from major writers such as Naguib Mahfouz (Egypt), Arundati Roy (India), Sinon Antoon (Iraq), Khalid Khalifa (Syria), and others. This emphasizes culturally relevant perspectives and issues shaping the post-modern MENA and subcontinent social realities. Specific foci include political, social, and religious life, colonialism and post-colonial rule, gender relations and military conflict(s). Attention will also be paid to literary styles and genres. Prerequisite: LIT 201.

LIT 410.title: Advanced Literary Theory
LIT 410.description: This course covers developments in literary theory from Ancient Greece to the 21st century. It defines and expands upon a wide range of theoretical approaches to various works of literature. Besides interpretive studies on and by Plato and Aristotle, a range of writers will be examined from Matthew Arnold, Walter Pater, Virginia Woolf, to Frederic Jameson, Roland Barthes, and Michel Foucault. The writings of Edward Said and Luce Irigaray will also be covered. Prerequisite: LIT 330.

LIT 421.title: Responses to the Land: Histories and Literatures of the Environment
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 421.description: Viewed predominantly through the lenses of poets, essayists, and historians, this course takes an interdisciplinary and cross-cultural approach to the questions posed by humankind’s relationship to the environments—natural and man-made—that we inhabit. The symbiotic relationship between humans and other living beings is given major emphasis in this course. Authors whose works are covered include Henry David Thoreau, Thomas Robert Malthus, Rachel Carson, Carl Sagan, Stephen Hawking and Jane Goodall.

LIT 431.title: Japanese Literature: Nara & Heian Eras
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 431.description: This course covers some of the Japanese earliest historical works such as the Kojiki, The Seventeen Article Constitution, Tale of Genji, and The Pillow Book. The course also treats selected Japanese poems and shorter works in some depth. By taking this course, the learners will begin to obtain a feel for Japanese literary sensibilities and conceptions of literature within the artistic domain. Prerequisite: LIT 330.

LIT 433.title: Persian Literature
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 433.description: This course focuses partly on Jalal ad-Din Rumi, the 13th century Persian poet, the love poems of Hafez e-Shirazi and the Shahnameh by Ferdowsi. This course offers a wide introductory survey to classical literature of Iran. Particular attention will be paid to rhetorical style, denotation and connotation in the works of these authors. Other forms of Persian literature will also be studied in order to develop a cross-cultural understanding of its varieties and sub-genres. Prerequisite: LIT 330.

LIT 441.title: Russian Society as Interpreted in Novels and Poetry
LIT 441.description: Individuals in all societies have always had to confront and survive injustice, corruption, indifference, and prejudice. The Russian authors were the pioneers in exposing these frightful realities with such accuracy, clarity and passion. These have become apparent in the literary and philosophic traditions of the Russian language. Select films adapted from these works shall be viewed. Authors include Leo Tolstoy, Feodor Dostoyevsky, Alexander Pushkin, Ivan Turgenev, Vladimir Nabokov, Nikolai Gogol, Boris Pasternak and others. Prerequisite: LIT 330.

LIT 451.title: American Woman Poets
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
LIT 451.description: This course features works by Emily Dickinson, Phillis Wheatley, Sylvia Plath, Adrienne Rich, Rita Dove and Sharon Olds. The learner examines how women poets commented upon and impacted the world in which they lived. This included the political establishment, the social and cultural realms. The course shows how their success in fighting societal norms to which they were expected to adhere has endured and still plays a large role today in Western political, social and professional life. Prerequisite: LIT 330.

MAT 101.title: College Algebra
MAT 101.description: This course introduces the basic concepts of algebra. Linear equations, inequalities, complex numbers, applications, and the graphs of linear and polynomial functions are explored.

MAT 101A.title: Advanced College Algebra
MAT 101A.description: This course provides the required algebraic background for Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) Majors. It covers essential algebraic concepts, including composition and inverses, graphs and transformations, algebraic functions, exponential and logarithmic functions, piecewise functions, operations on complex numbers, polynomial and rational equations, systems of equations and inequalities, and matrices and systems of linear equations.

MAT 102.title: Pre-calculus
MAT 102.description: Combines reviews of algebra, geometry, and functions into a preparatory course for calculus. Focuses on the mastery of critical skills necessary for success in subsequent math courses. Includes linear, quadratic, exponential, logarithmic, radical, polynomial, and rational functions; systems of equations; trigonometric ratios and functions; inverse trigonometric functions; applications of trigonometry, including vectors and laws of cosine and sine; polar functions and notation; and arithmetic of complex numbers.

MAT 111.title: Calculus and Analytic Geometry I
MAT 111.description: A detailed study of limits, continuity, derivatives of algebraic and transcendental functions, applications of derivatives, numerical techniques, integrals, and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

MAT 112.title: Calculus II
MAT 112.description: This course continues the integration techniques of elementary functions and their applications which started in MAT 111. It introduces and provides tests which used to check the convergence of infinite series. It covers the expansion of an analytic function in a convergent power series. The cases of separable and linear ordinary differential equations are studied as well as some of their applications mainly in population dynamics. Pre-requisite: MAT 111.

MAT 113.title: Calculus III
MAT 113.description: This course completes the standard Calculus sequence. It starts by discussing coordinate systems and vectors in 3-dimensions. It progresses to a discussion of the vector-valued functions and introduces geometric features of their images, such as the curvature and torsion of curves in 3 dimensions. The course moves on to the differential Calculus of functions of several real variables, discussing partial derivatives, the concept of differentiability, and the gradient, as well as their applications in determining unconstrained and constrained extrema, saddle points etc. It also introduces the infinitesimal operations of divergence and curl. The next topics are related to the integral calculus of functions of several variables, in particular double and triple integrals in the most commonly used coordinate systems. Line and surface integrals are also discussed. The course concludes with the basic theorems of vector analysis namely Green's, Stokes' and Gauss's theorems and discusses some of their applications. Pre-requisite: MAT 112.

MAT 130.title: Linear Algebra
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
MAT 130.description: This is a course about basic concepts of Linear Algebra as realized through concrete matrix calculations. The basic properties and operations of matrices, determinants and linear transformations are discussed, emphasizing their explicit applications. The general theoretical framework of Linear Algebra is discussed, but it is developed as far as it is directly related to explicit calculations involving matrices and determinants. The geometric interpretation of the structures and results developed algebraically is presented as far as possible. Pre-requisite: MAT 102 or Mathematics Assessment Test results above a certain cut-off.

MAT 202.title: Discrete Mathematics
MAT 202.description: The course introduces the fundamentals and use (abstract) of discrete structures, the backbones of computer science. Topics include logic, proof concepts, induction, relations, sets, introduction to graph theory, and functions. Prerequisite: Sophomore standing.

MAT 220.title: Ordinary Differential Equations
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
MAT 220.description: This course is a introduction to general methods for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and their associated initial value problems in the real domain. It includes the classification of ODEs, methods for solving first order order ODEs (exact, separable, linear), methods of obtaining general solutions of homogeneous and non-homogeneous higher order linear ODEs with constant coefficients, series solutions of linear ODEs, Laplace transforms and their application in solving linear ODEs, and methods for obtaining solutions of systems of linear ODEs. Pre-requisite: MAT 130. Co-requisite: MAT 113.

MGT 201.title: Principles of Management
MGT 201.description: This course will study the essential managerial functions of planning, organizing, staffing, directing, and controlling resources to accomplish organizational goals. The systems concept of management and the manager's role at each level of the organization are emphasized. Besides, a particular emphasis will be placed on the necessary skills for a manager to be effective. The course will involve an overview approach to covering the various concepts required to understand management’s role in the new organization. Management’s evolution as a distinct discipline will be covered. Prerequisite: BUS 112.

MGT 301.title: Business Ethics
MGT 301.description: Students explore the complex business environment and the relationships organizations have with civil society, the natural environment, and each other. Through this examination, students learn that ethical decision-making is critical to the successful management of any organization. The topics include primary and secondary stakeholder groups. An organizational stakeholder's impact on the groups' levels of responsibility consists of the biases, influences, and reasons that drive stakeholder perspectives, changing economic, political, social, and cultural forces and their impacts on business and society. A study of the continuum of socially responsible management and ethical business practices; and the challenges and opportunities that influence where an organization fits on the continuum will be revealed. Prerequisite: MGT 201.

MGT 310.title: Supply Chain Management
MGT 310.description: Logistics and supply chain management is an essential and integral part of any production process. This course's emphasis will be on illustrating the approaches for planning and designing for channels and effectively integrating suppliers, producers, and distributors in the supply chain. Case studies and experiential exercises will be used to illustrate the concepts and processes of supply chain management. Prerequisite: MGT 201.

PHA 101.title: Introduction to Pharmacy and Pharmaceutical Sciences
PHA 101.description: This course provides an overview of the profession of pharmacy and highlights the difference with pharmaceutical sciences and related specialties. It emphasizes upon the historical background and major milestones in the evolution of pharmacy from apothecaries to clinical pharmacy. It deals with pharmacy practice including major medical terms and abbreviations, functions of international pharmaceutical organizations, and drug classes and dosage forms. It also underscores the ethical principles, the nature and place of pharmaceutical services in the society, and the moral standards and professional conduct.

PHA 210.title: Introduction to Global Health
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHA 210.description: This course introduces students to the main concepts of global health and the factors associated with the gap between low-income countries and developed countries. It discusses the complex and critical link between global health and social and economic development. Class discussions will focus on strategies to address the challenges emerging in the global health spectrum.

PHA 300.title: Pharmacology I
PHA 300.description: This course covers the fundamental principles of pharmacology as well as the physiological, biochemical, and anatomical underpinnings of drug and chemical interactions with biological systems. It also covers the effects of medications and the mechanisms by which pharmaceuticals create therapeutic and harmful effects. Specific medications and pharmacological action sites are investigated further, starting with the peripheral nervous system, then the central nervous system, and finally drugs applied to treat inflammation.

PHA 300L.title: Pharmacology Laboratory
PHA 300L.description: A laboratory course that provides students with hands-on experience in the application of pharmacological principles. Students will learn to prepare and administer drugs, perform both in vitro and in vivo assays, and analyze data using statistical methods. Through a variety of experimental models and techniques, students will reinforce the concepts learned in the Pharmacology courses. This laboratory course is an essential component of the education of pharmacy students, providing them with the practical skills and knowledge necessary to succeed in the field of pharmacology. Pre-/co-requisite: PHA 300.

PHA 310.title: Dosage Forms I
PHA 310.description: This course discusses the design, formulation, manufacture, and evaluation of pharmaceutical dosage forms, based on physical and chemical principles. It also covers drug regulatory affairs (DRA), current good manufacturing practices (GMP), in compliance with FDA guidelines and standards. Compounding aqueous and non-aqueous solutions, powders and granules, capsules, and lozenges are also covered.

PHA 310L.title: Dosage Forms I Laboratory
PHA 310L.description: A laboratory course with hands-on practical applications for the procedures and principles utilized to generate and deliver individual extemporaneous prescriptions, including calculations and labeling of compounded dose forms. Pre-/co-requisite: PHA 320.

PHA 320.title: Medicinal Chemistry I
PHA 320.description: This course discusses the mechanism of action of drugs within organisms to design new and advanced pharmaceutical and medicinal agents. This interdisciplinary course also sheds the lights on the importance of knowledge obtained from toxicology, pharmacology, computer simulations, and clinical practice to offer valuable insights used in developing drugs with enhanced targeted actions and lower side effects.

PHA 330.title: Pharmaceutical Analysis
PHA 330.description: This course covers biotechnology and its applications in several medical, therapeutic, and scientific fields, with a concentration on pharmacy and pharmaceutical sciences. The fundamentals of recombinant DNA technology are discussed, with a focus on pharmaceutical applications, as well as the principles and techniques of spectroscopy and chromatography utilized in pharmaceutical analysis.

PHA 330L.title: Pharmaceutical Analysis Laboratory
PHA 330L.description: A laboratory course with hands-on practical applications that allow students to apply what they've learned in class to real-world situations. Pre-/co-requisite: PHA 340.

PHA 350.title: Pharmacology II
PHA 350.description: This course is a continuation of Pharmacology I. It covers medication classifications such as cardiovascular, anti-diabetic, and chemotherapy medicines. Specific medications and pharmacological action sites are investigated, starting with cardiovascular drugs, and moving on to antidiabetic agents, antifungal agents, antibiotics, and cancer chemotherapeutic agents. Pre-requisite: PHA 300.

PHA 360.title: Dosage Forms II
PHA 360.description: This course is a continuation of PHA 320. It focuses on the design, formulation, manufacturing, and evaluation of semi-solid, complex, and novel pharmaceutical dosage forms. Pre-requisite: PHA 320 and PHA 320L.

PHA 360L.title: Dosage Forms II Laboratory
PHA 360L.description: A laboratory course with hands-on practical applications for the formulation, preparation, handling and evaluation of colloidal dispersions, suspensions, emulsions, ointments, creams, suppositories, ophthalmic, otic and nasal preparations, and other topical products. Pre-/Co-requisite: PHA 360.

PHA 370.title: Medicinal Chemistry II
PHA 370.description: This course explores the main classes of prescription drugs including neurologic, anesthetic, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, antibacterial, and cardiovascular compounds. It also introduces the students to the indications of neurologic, anesthetic, analgesic, anti-inflammatory, anti-bacterial, and cardiovascular drugs, as well as their pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and pharmacological profiles. Pre-requisite PHA 330.

PHA 380.title: Pharmacotherapeutics I
PHA 380.description: This course covers the pathophysiology, etiology, risk factors and signs and symptoms of most common neurologic and psychiatric conditions. It also presents the use of pharmacologic and pharmacokinetic parameters, as well as the aspects that should be considered when choosing the optimal treatment alternatives. It also acquaints students with how to evaluate treatment therapy for psychiatric and neurologic illnesses by emphasizing monitoring parameters and significant pharmaceutical side effects. The student will use problem-solving techniques to patient-centered cases and design a treatment plan for the patient. Prerequisite PHA 300 and PHA 320

PHA 380L.title: Pharmacotherapeutics I: Applied Skills Lab
PHA 380L.description: Students enrolled in this applied pharmacotherapy lab will gain the skills necessary to provide care for patients with illnesses commonly encountered in community practice. Students will be afforded opportunities to provide patient-centered care utilizing the QuEST/SCHOLAR MACS process. Student achievement of core abilities will be assessed through an Objective Structured Clinical Examination. Co-Requisite: PHA 380

PHA 390.title: Drug Information and Literature Evaluation
PHA 390.description: This course covers the fundamentals of drug information such as medical terminologies and drug monographs. Students will learn how to recognize the various sections of a SOAP note. They will also learn how to prepare medication consultations and drug use reviews. The course will also help students to recognize the different types of literature materials, as well as how to apply basic biostatistics calculations.

PHA 395.title: Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience I (PPE I)
PHA 395.description: This course provides students with aspects of practical experiences in selected community or hospital pharmacy management settings under the supervision of pharmacists and clinical faculty preceptors. In compliance with Iraqi and US legislations, it focuses on community pharmacy management approaches and styles, organizational principles, personnel, purchasing and inventory control, pricing, para-pharmaceutical items, and community pharmacy services.

PHA 400.title: Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics
PHA 400.description: This course introduces the concepts of biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics. It emphasizes the absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion of pharmaceuticals to improve drug delivery system evaluation and patient management. Students will learn about the links between physiological parameters, compartmental models, pharmacokinetics, and pharmacodynamics to better comprehend the clinical variability of medication response.

PHA 400L.title: Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics Lab
PHA 400L.description: A laboratory course with hands-on practical and simulation applications that allow students to apply what they've learned in Pharmacokinetics and Biopharmaceutics course to real-world situations. Pre-/co-requisite: PHA 400

PHA 410L.title: Drug Design & Synthesis Lab
PHA 410L.description: A laboratory course with hands-on practical and simulation applications that allow students to apply what they've learned in Medicinal Chemistry I and II courses to real-world situations. Course Prerequisites: PHA 320 & PHA 370.

PHA 420.title: Pharmacotherapeutics II
PHA 420.description: This course covers the pathophysiology, etiology, risk factors and signs and symptoms of most common pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and rheumatological disorders with emphasis on monitoring parameters and the side effects of crucial medications. It introduces students to the use of pharmacologic and pharmacokinetic parameters, as well as the aspects that should be considered when selecting the optimal treatment alternatives. Students will use problem-solving techniques to patient-centered cases and design a treatment plan for the patient. Pre-requisite PHA 380

PHA 420L.title: Pharmacotherapeutics II: Applied Skills Lab
PHA 420L.description: This applied skills lab is associated with the pharmacotherapeutics course series and covers basic patient assessment and professional communication. Learning activities are designed to complement didactic instruction while allowing students to apply knowledge in a simulated environment. Student achievement of core abilities will be assessed through an Objective Structured Clinical Examination. One lab session is held weekly in correspondence with pharmacotherapeutics. Pre-requisite: PHA 380L. Co-Requisite: PHA 420

PHA 430.title: Pharmacotherapeutics III
PHA 430.description: This course covers the pathophysiology, etiology, risk factors and signs and symptoms of most common cardiovascular and renal disorders with emphasis on monitoring measures and significant pharmaceutical side effects. It introduces students to the use of pharmacologic and pharmacokinetic parameters, as well as the aspects that should be considered when selecting the optimal treatment alternatives. Students will use problem-solving techniques to patient-centered cases and design a treatment plan for the patient. Pre-requisite PHA 380

PHA 430L.title: Pharmacotherapeutics III: Applied Skills Lab
PHA 430L.description: Students enrolled in this applied pharmacotherapy lab will gain the skills necessary to provide care for patients with illnesses commonly encountered in pharmacy practice. Learning activities are designed to complement didactic instruction while allowing students to apply knowledge in a simulated environment. Students will be afforded opportunities to apply the Pharmacist's Patient Care Process thereby assessing and therapeutically managing patients. Student achievement of core abilities will be assessed through an Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE). Co-Requisite: PHA 430

PHA 440.title: Toxicology
PHA 440.description: This course presents the fundamentals of toxicology covering areas of toxicology, human toxicity factors, and toxin disposal in the body. The course also teaches students how to diagnose poisonings and how to treat them clinically (i.e., stabilization of vital functions and specialized antidotal methods). The mechanism of toxicity, sources of exposure, primary clinical manifestations, and therapeutic options for poisoning with common chemical groups (pesticides, metals, solvents, and common medications) will be discussed.

PHA 450.title: Dispensing and Pharmaceutical Care
PHA 450.description: This highly interactive practice course is designed to teach students the proper techniques and skills required to dispense drug products safely and accurately to patients in community and hospital settings. Students will also learn to effectively counsel patients, manage any conflict that may arise between the pharmacists, other healthcare professionals, and patients, and develop leadership skills. This course also teaches students to assist patients in the safe, appropriate, effective, and cost-efficient use of nonprescription medications.

PHA 460.title: Pharmacognosy
PHA 460.description: This course introduces students to natural products and other bioactive agents from nature as well as their origins, identification, development, and application. It also identifies the chemical structure, classifications, and structure-activity connections of natural products. Furthermore, the course emphasizes the importance of natural products as major ingredients in medicine development.

PHA 495.title: Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience II (PPE II)
PHA 495.description: This course provides students with practical experiences in hospital settings through the provision of drug information services to other healthcare providers. Students will learn how to screen and intervene on hospital medication orders, as well as hospital pharmacy accreditation criteria, hospital pharmacy administration, policies, and procedures, and drug distribution systems and patient-centered pharmacy services. As per site requirements, they will also assist in the preparation of a medication monograph, addressing drug information queries, assessing adverse drug responses, analyzing clinical studies, and participating in drug utilization reviews. Pre-requisite PHA 395

PHA 500.title: Pharmacoeconomics and Drug Marketing
PHA 500.description: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of pharmacoeconomic evaluation and pharmaceutical marketing. Topics include cost-effectiveness analysis, drug pricing, market access, branding, and promotion strategies, with a focus on applications in healthcare systems and the pharmaceutical industry. Emphasis is placed on regional practices and policies within the Middle East. By the end of the course, students will be able to assess the economic value of therapies and design basic marketing strategies for pharmaceutical products.

PHA 510.title: Advanced Clinical Diagnostics
PHA 510.description: This course prepares pharmacy students to interpret and apply clinical laboratory and diagnostic data in patient-centered care. Through case-based and team-based lectures, students will develop clinical reasoning and decision-making skills. Laboratory sessions focus on hands-on experience in microbiology, clinical biochemistry, and applied skills techniques, ensuring pharmacists are equipped to participate in multidisciplinary healthcare environments. Pre-requisite: PHA 470; PHA 480

PHA 520.title: Clinical Pharmacokinetics
PHA 520.description: This course builds on foundational pharmacokinetics by focusing on the clinical application of drug dosing and monitoring. Students will study key topics including hepatic clearance, protein binding (PPB), and pharmacokinetic variability in special populations. The course emphasizes therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) and individualized dose adjustment for critical drugs such as digoxin, aminoglycosides, theophylline, and anticonvulsants. Through case-based learning, students will develop the skills necessary to apply pharmacokinetic principles to optimize therapy, minimize toxicity, and enhance patient outcomes in clinical practice. Pre-requisite: Pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutics (PHA 400), Pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutics (PHA 400L)

prerequisites.text: Pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutics (PHA 400), Pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutics (PHA 400L)

PHA 530.title: Quality Assurance
PHA 530.description: The Quality Assurance course introduces pharmacy students to the core principles of pharmaceutical quality systems. It covers GMP, QA, QC, and relevant ISO standards, along with key concepts such as quality definitions, validation, calibration, and documentation. The course provides a solid foundation for understanding how quality is maintained and regulated within the pharmaceutical industry. Pre-requisite: Dosage forms-II (PHA 360), Pharmacokinetics and biopharmaceutics (PHA 400)

PHA 545.title: Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience III (PPE III)
PHA 545.description: This practical course will allow future pharmacists to evaluate, analyze, and devise a treatment plan after acquiring all required information from patients and healthcare professionals and conducting a literature review with a focus on main literature and treatment guidelines. Students will also gain expertise in the following pharmacy functions: reviewing patient profiles for drug interactions, medication noncompliance, and inappropriate drug therapy; counseling; knowledge of drug generic, brand names and dosage forms available on the market; reviewing patient profiles for drug interactions, medication noncompliance, and inappropriate drug therapy; basic administrative skills. Pre-requisite PHA 495

PHA 550.title: Pharmaco-genomics
PHA 550.description: This course introduces a new genetic-based therapeutics profession that aims to influence and revolutionize pharmacy practice. It also introduces the fundamentals of molecular genetics and how genetics may be utilized to explain medication response variability, in addition to the pharmacogenetics of drug transport and metabolism, as well as their significance to clinical practice and drug therapy individualization. It also looks at existing and potential pharmacogenomics applications in oncology, hematology, cardiovascular and neurological illnesses, organ transplantation, and other fields.

PHA 560.title: Pharmacoepidemiology & Pharmacovigilance
PHA 560.description: This course introduces pharmacoepidemiology as a foundation for understanding and critically evaluating studies in scientific literature. Students will explore fundamental epidemiological concepts, study designs, data sources, and statistical methods relevant to pharmacoepidemiology. The role of pharmacoepidemiology in pharmacy practice, including bias, confounding, causality, and pharmaco-economic principles, will also be covered.

PHA 570.title: Pharmacy Law & Regulation
PHA 570.description: This course introduces students to the legal and regulatory framework governing the practice of pharmacy in Iraq and key international pharmacy laws, with comparisons to international standards. The course covers the principles of pharmaceutical legislation, regulatory compliance, and professional ethics. Emphasis is placed on the role of the pharmacist within national health law, drug control regulations, licensing procedures, controlled substances, pharmacy practice standards, and the Iraqi Ministry of Health guidelines.

PHA 580.title: Pharmacotherapeutics VI
PHA 580.description: This course enables students to develop knowledge regarding the pathophysiology of the most common cancer diseases, risk factors, prevention, and treatment approaches based on updated guidelines. Students will use problem-solving techniques to patient-centered cases and design a treatment plan for the patient. Prerequisite: PHA 480

PHA 581.title: Clinical Nutrition and Diet Therapy
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHA 581.description: This course provides students with a fundamental understanding of nutrients and the role of nutrition in disease prevention and treatment. It also instructs students on the pathological states of patients with nutrition-related chronic diseases, as well as their unique nutritional needs. Students will also gain advanced evidence-based and practice-based knowledge on formulating, developing, monitoring, and administering disease- and patient-specific parenteral and enteral nutrition, as well as enhancing the pharmacist's role in nutrition support therapy

PHA 584.title: Industrial pharmacy-I
notices: This course has not been scheduled.
PHA 584.description: Industrial Pharmacy I introduces pharmacy students to the foundational principles of pharmaceutical manufacturing. The course covers essential topics including pre-formulation studies, material handling, basic production processes, packaging, stability studies, and safety measures. Students will also learn about the layout of pharmaceutical manufacturing facilities, including sterile areas. Basic unit operation concepts such as mixing, granulation, drying, and tableting are introduced, providing a foundation for more advanced study in subsequent courses focusing on unit operations in pharmaceutical manufacturing.

PHA 585.title: Industrial pharmacy-II
PHA 585.description: Industrial Pharmacy II explores advanced unit operations in pharmaceutical manufacturing. The course covers essential processes such as film coating, distillation, heat transfer, extraction, filtration, centrifugation, and drying. Students will gain an in-depth understanding of the principles and techniques behind these operations and their application in large-scale pharmaceutical production. The course emphasizes optimizing these processes for efficiency and practical use in the manufacturing of pharmaceutical products. Through case studies and practical sessions, students will develop the skills needed to manage and troubleshoot various unit operations in the pharmaceutical industry.

PHA 595.title: Introductory Pharmacy Practice Experience IV (IPPE IV)
PHA 595.description: The fourth IPPE consists of the student's choice to do a follow-up community rotation, specialized hospital rotation, academic rotation, administrative, or industry rotation. The students will participate in day-to-day activities determined by their preceptor and preceptor sight and will apply their pharmacy knowledge to different projects. This rotation will consist of a minimum of 480 hours. Student Pharmacists will be evaluated by the pharmacy preceptor and the clinical coordinator at the mid and end points of their practice experience.

PHA 597.title: Graduation Project
PHA 597.description: The Pharmacy Graduation Project provides students with the opportunity to independently explore a topic of interest within the field of pharmacy under faculty supervision. Students are expected to apply principles of scientific inquiry, critical thinking, and professional communication to design, conduct, and present a scholarly project. This experience is intended to develop students’ research, analytical, and writing skills while fostering ethical and evidence-based professional practice.

PHI 101.title: Introduction to Ethics
PHI 101.description: An introduction to the philosophical study of morality (ethics), the ideas of right and wrong behaviors, and answers to ethical questions by well-known philosophers. Students will develop abilities to read, write, explicate, analyze, and evaluate philosophical literature and to express well one’s own ethical positions, thinking critically and analytically about ethical issues.
